quote: the blazing flame that had blinded me
context: At the end of Canto 25, Dante stared into John's light to see whether the apostle had his body in Heaven, and lost his sight. Still blind, he is now examined by John on love.
The third of Dante's three examinations in this heaven. Peter tested him on faith (Canto 24) and James on hope (Canto 25). John asks what Dante loves, and why.

note: The blindness is temporary. It is often read as a lesson: love of God must be professed before it can be seen, and sight comes back stronger once the profession is made.

The disciple in Damascus who laid his hands on Saul, the future Saint Paul, and cured the blindness that struck him on the road (Acts 9). Beatrice's eyes will do for Dante what those hands did for Paul.
In the love poetry of Dante's youth, love enters through the eyes. He first saw Beatrice as a child in Florence, and says the fire has burned ever since.
Heaven, pictured throughout Paradiso as the court of a king. The Good that contents it is God.

The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet: the beginning and the end. "I am Alpha and Omega" is God's saying in the Book of Revelation, which tradition gave to John himself. Dante answers the apostle in the apostle's own words: God is the start and goal of everything he loves.
The first answer was too general. John wants the reasons: what taught Dante to aim his love at God.
Dante names two teachers: human reason, meaning philosophy, and the authority that comes down from Heaven, meaning the Bible. He gives the argument from reason first.

quote: Good, insofar as it is good
note: The argument in brief. Whatever is seen to be good is loved, and the greater the good, the greater the love. God is the highest good, the source of all others. So anyone who sees this clearly must love God most.

Usually taken to be Aristotle, who taught that the first mover moves the heavens by being loved and desired. Some commentators have proposed Plato or the writer known as Dionysius instead. Dante does not name him.
The angels, and in some readings the heavens they turn. Their first love is God.

context: God's words to Moses on Mount Sinai (Exodus 33:19), when Moses asked to see his glory. God calls himself all goodness.

note: Most readers take this as the opening of John's Gospel: "In the beginning was the Word". Others think it is the Book of Revelation, where God is called Alpha and Omega. Either way Dante cites his examiner's own writing to him.
John has the reasons of the mind. Now he asks for the rest: everything else that pulls Dante's heart toward God.
Love as something that bites and holds. The image is deliberately rough for so high a subject.

John. The four Gospel writers were each given a symbol from the four winged creatures of Ezekiel and Revelation. John's is the eagle, the bird that flies highest and was said to look straight at the sun.

quote: The existence of the world and my own existence
note: The "bites" are God's gifts, each a reason for love: the creation of the world, Dante's own life, Christ's death for him, and the promise of Heaven.

quote: that which all believers hope for
note: The joy of Heaven: the hope Dante defined for Saint James in Canto 25.

Love aimed at the wrong things, or at lesser goods in the wrong measure: the root of all sin, as Virgil explained in Purgatorio 17. The image recalls the first simile of the poem, the swimmer who reaches shore and looks back at the deadly water (Inferno 1).

All creatures. The garden is the world, and God its gardener, an image from John's Gospel (15:1). Dante loves each creature according to how much good God has put in it, which is how charity extends to one's neighbor.
The song of the angels around God's throne in Isaiah 6 and in Revelation 4. It tells Dante he has passed. Beatrice sings with the rest.
Medieval medicine explained sight by a fine "spirit" that ran along the nerve to the eye. The "layers" are the eye's membranes, through which light was thought to pass one by one.
Three lights have been with Dante since Canto 25: Peter, James and John. A fourth has joined them while he was blind.

context: Adam appears beside the three apostles. Dante has four questions for him, and Adam, who reads them in God, answers without being asked.

quote: O fruit that was brought forth
note: Dante's word is "pomo", an apple or fruit. Adam alone was created full grown, never a child. The word also glances at the fruit he ate.
Every woman descends from Adam, and every woman who marries takes one of his sons for a husband. So each bride is both to him.
A homely comparison that has surprised readers: an animal under a cloth, whose movements show through it. Adam is hidden inside his light, and its stirring shows his gladness.
God. The blessed see every thought reflected in him before it is spoken. Everything else mirrors God only partly, and nothing can hold a full image of him.
Adam lists Dante's four questions: when he was created, how long he stayed in Eden, what his sin really was, and what language he spoke. He answers the third first.

context: Where Adam was placed at his creation, and where Beatrice came to meet Dante and readied him for the climb through the heavens (Purgatorio 28–33).

note: God's anger at the first sin, which shut humankind out of Eden and of Heaven until Christ's death.
The sin was not appetite for a fruit. It was pride and disobedience: going past the limit God had set. Readers often compare Ulysses in Inferno 26, who sailed past the limit set for sailors.

quote: the place where your Lady summoned Virgil
context: Adam waited here from his death until Christ came down and freed him. Beatrice came to this same place to send Virgil to Dante's aid (Inferno 2).

quote: four thousand three hundred and two
note: Adam's years in Limbo. Added to the 930 years of his life, they put the Crucifixion 5,232 years after the Creation. The figure follows the Christian chronologies of Dante's day, which were built on the ages given in the Bible.
One trip of the sun through the twelve signs of the zodiac: a year. Genesis 5:5 gives Adam's age at death as 930.

Dante changes his mind here. In his earlier treatise on language, De vulgari eloquentia, he wrote that Adam spoke Hebrew, a language made by God that lasted unchanged until the Tower of Babel. Now Adam says he made his language himself, and that it died out naturally, as all languages do.

context: The "impossible work" is the Tower of Babel, which could never have reached heaven. Adam says his own language had vanished long before the confusion of tongues there.

note: The turning stars were thought to shape human moods and tastes. As they change, so does what people like, including how they speak.
A Hebrew name for God. Many modern editions of the Italian text read "I" here, a single letter, and take El as the later name. The point is the same in both: even the name of God changed over time.
Hebrew for "my God", the word Christ cries from the cross in Matthew's Gospel.
From the Roman poet Horace, who wrote in his Art of Poetry that words are like a forest's leaves: the old fall and new ones grow.

quote: the mountain that rises highest above the waters
context: The Garden of Eden stands on its summit, in the middle of the southern ocean.

note: Adam's whole stay in Eden, before the sin and after it, until he was driven out.

quote: from the first hour until the one that follows
note: Hours were counted from sunrise, so the sixth ends at noon, when the sun passes into the next quarter of the sky. Adam was in Paradise from dawn until just after midday: little more than six hours.
